ideal-op-amp.L1: States the two rules of the ideal op-amp, equal input voltages and no input current, and the gains −R₂/R₁ and 1 + R₂/R₁, with notes open.
ideal-op-amp.L2: Applies the inverting, non-inverting and follower formulas to find v_out, and solves those three circuits with the two rules.
ideal-op-amp.L3: Solves an unfamiliar op-amp circuit with the recipe (V₊ = V₋, no input current, KCL at the pinned node); explains the virtual short as the output moving until the inputs agree, so v₊ − v₋ = v_out/A; predicts the gain error from 1/(1 + Aβ).
ideal-op-amp.L4: Checks that the feedback is negative and the output inside the rails before using the virtual short; estimates the error of a finite-gain op-amp; says when input current or output resistance stops being negligible.
missteps: uses the virtual short in a circuit with positive feedback or a saturated output
lets current flow into the op-amp's inputs when writing KCL
treats the virtual short as a wire and sends current through it
takes the non-inverting gain as R₂/R₁
computes β with the wrong resistor on top

seeds.predict: An inverting amplifier with a given R₁ and R₂ whose op-amp's A falls by a factor of ten: by how much does the gain change?
seeds.explain: Why the − input of an inverting amplifier sits at ground although nothing connects it to ground.
seeds.limit: Raise v_in until the output reaches a rail: what happens to v₋, and why does the recipe stop working?
seeds.transfer: A summing amplifier with two inputs through two resistors into one node: find v_out with the recipe.

operating-point.L1: States that the bias (Q) point is the DC solution with all signals off, and that it fixes the small-signal parameters.
operating-point.L2: Finds I_D, V_GS and V_DS of a common-source stage with the square law and checks the region.
operating-point.L3: Explains why the bias is found first and how it sets g_m and r_o; predicts what moving V_GS or W/L does to I_D, V_DS and the region; sees when the drain sits too close to the edge of saturation for the swing it must carry.
operating-point.L4: Chooses a bias for gain and swing together: low V_OV for gain per current, enough V_DS headroom, and a signal small next to V_OV; knows the bias drifts with V_T and temperature and why circuits fix the current instead.
missteps: uses the small-signal model without checking that the transistor is in saturation
solves the bias with the signal still applied
assumes saturation without checking V_DS ≥ V_OV

seeds.predict: A common-source stage biased in saturation; V_GS is raised by 0.2 V. What happens to I_D, V_DS and the region?
seeds.explain: Why the bias point has to be found before any small-signal number can be written down.
seeds.limit: Raise V_GS until the stage leaves saturation: at which V_GS, and what happens to the gain?
seeds.transfer: A sensor that drifts the DC level on the gate by 50 mV: what does that do to g_m and to the gain, and how would you bias to make it matter less?

small-signal-analysis.L1: Lists the steps: find the bias, replace each device by its model, turn DC sources off, solve the linear circuit.
small-signal-analysis.L2: Carries out the steps on a common-source stage: draws the small-signal circuit and writes A_v = −g_m(r_o ∥ R_D).
small-signal-analysis.L3: Explains the model as the tangent to the device curve at the bias point; says why a DC voltage source becomes a short and a DC current source an open; says what "small" is measured against and estimates the error from v̂/(4V_OV).
small-signal-analysis.L4: Knows when the method fails (large signals, a bias near a region edge, a signal that crosses into cut-off) and switches to large-signal analysis there; uses superposition of bias and signal knowing it holds only for the linearised circuit.
missteps: uses the small-signal model without checking that the transistor is in saturation
treats g_m as a constant of the transistor instead of a function of the bias
leaves a DC source in the small-signal circuit, or turns a DC current source into a short
measures "small" against V_DD instead of V_OV

seeds.predict: A stage with A_v = −6; the input amplitude goes from 10 mV to 200 mV with V_OV = 0.3 V. Is the output still 6 times the input, and which half of the wave suffers?
seeds.explain: Why a DC supply is a ground in the small-signal circuit.
seeds.limit: The signal amplitude raised toward V_OV: which way does the output wave distort, and why?
seeds.transfer: A circuit with a DC current source as the load: draw its small-signal circuit and say what the source becomes.
